turns.t: Good morning. Forgive me, am I right in thinking you are the doctor who deals with nerves, or have I come to the wrong room?
You're in the right place. I'm the neurologist. What's the trouble?
Thank you. It's my legs, I'm afraid. In the evenings they become quite impossible to keep still.
Describe the feeling for me.
A sort of crawling, creeping sensation deep inside, from the knee down to the ankle. Moving is the only relief. I have to get up and walk about the kitchen.
How long has this been going on?
About four months, I should say, though it has been worse since the spring.
How often does it come?
Nearly every night. Most evenings from around nine o'clock.
And what does it do to your sleep?
Rather a lot, I'm afraid. I lie awake for an hour or two before I can drop off, and then I am exhausted in the daytime. I nodded off over my book only yesterday afternoon.
Does anything make it worse, as far as you have noticed?
A strong cup of coffee after dinner, I think. I have a weakness for it. And sitting through the evening news.
Any numbness, weakness in the legs, or back pain?
No, none of those. Nothing of that sort at all.
Right. Now, the background. Any other conditions I should know about?

Well, I have high blood pressure, eight years now. And acid reflux. And arthritis in my knees, although that is more of a nuisance than anything. Oh, and migraines. I thought I had grown out of them, but I still get one once in a while.
Which tablets do you take for those?
The amlodipine, 5 milligrams every morning, for the blood pressure. And a small white tablet for the stomach acid, at night. I am so sorry, I can never remember what it is called.
Don't worry, the pharmacy list will tell us. Do you have any allergies to medicines?
Yes, penicillin. I came out in a rash all over when I was given it, years ago.
Noted, thank you. Have you had any operations?
I had my gallbladder removed, about twelve years ago.
Does anyone in your family have leg trouble like this, or other nerve conditions?
My mother had restless legs, quite badly, in her seventies. And my brother has diabetes, though I don't suppose that is relevant.
Do you smoke, and how much alcohol do you drink?
I have never smoked. I drink a glass of wine on Saturdays, no more than that.
Right. I'd like the nurse to take your observations before I examine you.
Of course. If you would roll up your sleeve for me. That's lovely. Blood pressure is 138/84 mmHg.
Pulse is 72 bpm. Temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
And you weigh 71 kilograms with your shoes off.
Thank you, nurse. Mrs Okonjo-Reyes, any trouble passing water?
No, that is all quite normal, thank you.
Let me look at your legs now. Lie back on the couch for me.
Certainly.
Reflexes are normal at the knees and ankles. Strength is normal in both legs, and there is no swelling around the ankles.
Is that good?

Yes, that's reassuring. So, here is what I think. This looks most likely to be restless legs syndrome. Your mother's history and the evening pattern both fit. I can't rule out low iron as a contributor, though, which is a common trigger, so we should check.
I see. What would you suggest?

Three things. One, a blood test for your iron stores, which I'll arrange today. Two, cut the coffee after dinner, and try a warm bath and some calf stretching before bed. Three, there are medicines for this, but I would rather not start one until the bloods are back.
Might I give up coffee entirely?
Nothing after lunchtime would be the aim. And please bring the packet of your stomach tablet next time, so we can identify it.
I shall do that.
If the bloods are normal and your sleep is still being wrecked, I might consider a nerve conduction study, to test the nerves in your legs and be thorough.
What does that involve?
Small electrical pulses through some sticky pads. Slightly odd, but not painful.
That sounds tolerable.
Now, if it isn't better in six weeks, come back and see me. Sooner if the legs become weak or numb.
And if the bloods show something?
Then we treat that first, which is exactly why we do them first.
Thank you, doctor. You have been most thorough.
Good luck with the coffee. The nurse will show you where to have the blood taken.
This way, please, Mrs Okonjo-Reyes.
